mcqs.question: In cloud IAM, what's the relationship between a policy and a role?
options: A policy is a named collection of roles that can be assumed
A role is a named bundle of permissions; a policy defines the actual rules (allowed actions on allowed resources) that get attached to that role
They are two names for the exact same concept with no meaningful difference
A policy can only be attached to a human user, never to a role
mcqs.explanation: A policy is the rule set; a role is the named bundle you can hand out that carries those rules, and any identity — human or workload — can assume that role. Policies aren't restricted to human users, and treating role and policy as identical concepts misses the layering that makes IAM reusable across different identity types.

mcqs.question: An identity has one policy that allows deleting a resource and a second policy that explicitly denies deleting that same resource. What happens?
options: The delete is denied — an explicit deny overrides any explicit allow, regardless of how many other policies grant it
The delete is allowed, because at least one policy grants it
The system throws an error and no action is evaluated
The most recently attached policy wins, whichever it is
mcqs.explanation: Standard cloud IAM evaluation gives explicit deny precedence over any explicit allow — it's the mechanism that lets you write an unbreakable exception no other grant can override. There's no policy-evaluation error state for this case, and precedence isn't based on attachment order.

mcqs.question: Why is a leaked long-lived IAM access key generally more dangerous than a leaked role-assumption credential?
options: Role-assumption credentials cannot be used to access any cloud resources at all
Long-lived keys always have broader permissions than any role can have
A long-lived key stays valid until someone manually notices and revokes it, while a role credential expires automatically, often within an hour, limiting the exposure window
Long-lived keys are stored with stronger encryption than role credentials
mcqs.explanation: The security advantage of roles is the short, automatic expiry — a leaked long-lived key can be exploited for as long as it takes someone to notice, which is often months. Role credentials work fully within their scope while valid, permission breadth is independent of key type, and encryption-at-rest strength isn't the relevant distinction here.

mcqs.question: In a cross-account IAM setup, what does the role's trust policy in account B actually control?
options: Which specific actions the assumed role is permitted to perform once assumed
Whether account A's own IAM policies are automatically copied into account B
How long the underlying compute instance in account A can run
Which outside identities or accounts are permitted to assume that role in the first place
mcqs.explanation: A trust policy is specifically about who is allowed to assume the role — a separate concern from the permissions policy that defines what the role can do once assumed. It has nothing to do with compute lifetime in the calling account, and policies are never auto-copied between accounts.

mcqs.question: A role was scoped correctly to least privilege a year ago. Why might it no longer actually be least-privilege today, even with no deliberate change to its intent?
options: IAM policies automatically expand their scope after a fixed time period
Least-privilege policies degrade once a role is assumed more than a certain number of times
Cloud providers periodically add default permissions to every existing role
Permission drift — temporary grants added during incidents or feature work tend to accumulate and rarely get removed once the immediate need passes
mcqs.explanation: Roles accumulate permissions over time as temporary or one-off grants outlive their original need and nothing forces a review, which is exactly why access reviews and permission-usage auditing need to be recurring, not one-time. IAM policies don't self-expand, providers don't silently add permissions to existing roles, and assumption frequency has no bearing on scope.

mcqs.question: A developer attaches a wildcard admin policy to a service "temporarily" to unblock a permissions error, intending to scope it down later. Why does this pattern account for so many real-world over-permissioned roles?
options: Because wildcard policies are technically impossible to remove once attached
Because cloud providers require a minimum 90-day lifetime on any admin policy
Because nothing breaks while the wildcard grant is in place, so there's no forcing function that makes anyone come back and tighten it
Because scoping down a policy always requires provider support intervention
mcqs.explanation: The absence of any visible breakage removes the pressure to revisit the shortcut, so a genuinely temporary fix quietly becomes permanent — this is why treating broad grants as requiring an explicit, tracked follow-up matters. Wildcard policies can be removed at any time by the account owner, there's no provider-mandated minimum lifetime, and scoping down never requires provider support.
